Sampled HR@10 measures ranking against the sampled candidates, not full-catalog HR@10. Krichene and Rendle show that sampling can reverse model comparisons even in expectation; a narrow confidence interval cannot remove this bias. For this benchmark, retain the pinned 99 negatives and evaluator, and describe results explicitly as 100-candidate validation HR@10. [On Sampled Metrics for Item Recommendation](https://research.google/pubs/on-sampled-metrics-for-item-recommendation/)

Paired bootstrap resampling preserves the correspondence between two systems’ evaluation outcomes. Applied here: store each model’s per-user hit indicator; resample the same user indices for both models within each category, retaining 200 users/category; calculate each category’s mean hit difference and average the four differences equally. Repeat, for example, 10,000 times and report the 2.5th–97.5th percentiles. This proposed adaptation estimates user-sampling uncertainty conditional on the trained models and fixed candidates; it does not capture training-seed or candidate-sampling variability. [Koehn’s paired-bootstrap method](https://aclanthology.org/W04-3250/)

Repeated hyperparameter and checkpoint selection can overfit a finite validation set, making the winning score optimistic. Ordinary bootstrap intervals computed after selecting the winner do not correct that selection bias. Keep selection based on the required macro validation HR@10; report trial/checkpoint counts, category scores, and paired differences against a predefined baseline. Treat intervals as descriptive evidence rather than proof that the selected winner generalizes; leave hidden-test assessment to the host. [Cawley and Talbot](https://www.jmlr.org/beta/papers/v11/cawley10a.html)
